recent_posts.title: Four components you need to build an AI agent
recent_posts.summary: A practical breakdown of the four core components needed to build an AI agent: RAG (Retrieval Augmented Generation), tool calling, memory management, and feedback loops. Includes a concrete example using Anthropic's Python SDK tool_runner, explains how tool calling enables iterative data retrieval, covers memory compaction strategies for long sessions, and discusses feedback mechanisms including human-in-the-loop approaches.

recent_posts.title: Quick note on evals and putting AI in your resume
recent_posts.summary: When hiring engineers who list AI on their resume, the most revealing question is whether they used evals to measure improvements. Building AI-powered features means working with stochastic systems, so you need a structured way to know if version 2 performs better than version 1. The approach: build a dataset from real user behavior, create a test suite to run against different models and prompts, maintain a human-in-the-loop fallback, and continuously feed failures back into the dataset. This eval discipline is the real competitive moat — everyone has access to the same models, but your proprietary dataset and domain expertise are what differentiate your product.

recent_posts.title: What I learned after AI wrote 97% of my production code
recent_posts.summary: A senior engineer at a near-billion-dollar company shares that AI (via Cursor) now writes 97% of their production code, including high-stakes systems like an invoicing platform. The key workflow: use Cursor background agents via Slack, don't watch them work, provide clear context and desired outcomes in prompts, then iterate with code review just like you would with a human engineer. The author dismisses elaborate prompt engineering tricks (Agents.md, plan mode, etc.) as distractions, arguing the fundamentals — speak clearly, give context, iterate — are what actually matter. A cautionary note: long-running agents that make early mistakes can produce thousands of lines of broken code, echoing the failures of waterfall development.

recent_posts.title: Why reading academic papers is the most efficient way to learn
recent_posts.summary: Reading academic papers is an underrated way to quickly gain deep knowledge in any technical field. By reading Claude Shannon's original information theory paper, the author was able to distill an entire college course down to one core formula. Similarly, spending a few hours reading papers on agentic AI development provided a solid mental framework for the current state of the field. Papers are best for distilled knowledge, while in-person expert conversations are better for cutting-edge info not yet published, and books work best for entering entirely new fields.

recent_posts.title: How watching users work reveals what engineers should actually build
recent_posts.summary: A practical technique for engineers to build better software: sit with users or support staff and watch them work for an hour. This 'frustration-driven development' approach surfaces hidden bugs, missing features, broken workflows, and misaligned assumptions that would never appear in a ticket or spec. Real examples from three sessions include a missing button that support had been working around for months, a finance team running a multi-hour process across 6 pages in 3 tools, and discovering that adding more info to support tickets wasn't actually the bottleneck. The key insight is to find the biggest levers — often automation or better self-service — rather than patching symptoms.

recent_posts.title: Frustration Driven Development
recent_posts.summary: Frustration is a powerful engineering signal. Instead of repeatedly doing the same manual task, great engineers use that annoyance as motivation to eliminate the problem permanently. Three concrete examples illustrate this: upgrading CI/CD runners to cut build times from 10 to 2 minutes instead of endless Slack debates; building a self-serve permissions UI so managers can grant roles without engineering involvement; and writing AI-assisted tests to cover complex invoicing edge cases that were impossible to reproduce manually. The core philosophy is that your job is to remove work, not just do it — build tools, scripts, dashboards, and automation that create durable value and eliminate recurring friction.

recent_posts.title: Software engineer interviews for the age of AI
recent_posts.summary: A hiring manager shares how software engineering interviews should evolve in the AI era. Rather than LeetCode puzzles, the approach focuses on three stages: a screening conversation that probes fractal knowledge depth about past projects, a system design interview that reveals hands-on vs. theoretical understanding, and a practical coding exercise using a real stubbed codebase where AI tools are explicitly encouraged. The coding interview tests whether candidates can navigate ambiguity, ask business questions, read documentation, and ship working code with AI assistance — not just generate plausible-looking output. The core argument is that AI raises the bar: engineers must own and be accountable for the systems they build, so interviews should test judgment and problem-solving depth, not typing speed or memorized algorithms.

recent_posts.title: Stop obsessing over your AI setup and just ship code
recent_posts.summary: A short opinion piece arguing that the best engineers focus on shipping working software rather than obsessing over AI tool setups, productivity systems, or elaborate orchestration frameworks. The core message is outcomes over outputs: what matters is what gets shipped to production and what users can do, not how sophisticated your tooling is. Uses analogies like Moneyball and Jeff Atwood's classic anti-TODO post to reinforce the point.

recent_posts.title: How engineers can learn to handle chaos and interruptions
recent_posts.summary: Handling chaos in software engineering is a learnable skill built on attitude and habits. Engineers should own their systems, develop a long-term vision, break work into small shippable increments, and avoid panic during incidents. Key practices include cutting scope rather than corners, focusing ruthlessly on high-impact work, and triaging production issues calmly by assessing real severity before acting. The goal is to keep delivering value even when priorities shift or emergencies arise.

recent_posts.title: Put scope on your resume
recent_posts.summary: When reviewing resumes, job titles carry little weight compared to scope — what you actually did, for whom, and what impact it had. Promotions and upward progression are strong signals, but the real differentiator is demonstrating concrete results: team size managed, technical impact delivered, or business metrics moved. A useful shorthand is framing your tenure in terms of company ARR or headcount growth, which gives hiring managers precise context regardless of company size or title inflation.
